how: Each feed page was read in his Brave through Claude in Chrome: the result's fields and the SHA-256 of its checked text, and its windows as compact lines (WINDOWS-A.txt, WINDOWS-B.txt, each checked against the page's own SHA-256 of that line). The checked text is rebuilt from the pasted payload (tools/humanization/substack_check_text.py) with two changes that this paste needed to reach the page's SHA-256:   - Substack showed a straight double quote after "(" or "—" as a closing quote (four places: Céline's song, the porch     story's "Once upon a time", the photos' "You hated that coat", and "I hate cooking"), where the tool's rule makes it     an opening one;   - half B's embedded note reads as one line, its body with curly apostrophes, given here as NOTE_LINE. Then every item of round 6 (experiments/t107-substack/ITEMS.json) is found in its half's checked text, its words in AI windows are counted, and each prediction (ledger #262 to #280) gets its result. Writes RESULT-A.json, RESULT-B.json, TEXT-A.txt, TEXT-B.txt (the checked texts) and ROUND6-RESULTS.json; --ledger also records the results.

ai_windows.text: If picturing your little one feels fake, like you’re just making it up, a real photo of you as a child can help, since there’s no face or posture to invent.
Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine.
Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started.
I wouldn’t trust a model more just because there’s a big institute behind it handing out certificates.
